title: Pragmatic AI with TypeChat: Daniel Rosenwasser
talk_summary: Daniel Rosenwasser presents TypeChat, a library that uses TypeScript type definitions to both guide an LLM's output and validate it, with validation errors fed back to the model for repair. He extends the idea from JSON extraction to generated programs, using a JSON-based 'fake language' with refs to prior results, compiled to an in-memory TypeScript program so only allowed methods and type-correct arguments are accepted.

takeaways.technique: Schema-guided output with typed validation and repair loop
takeaways.what_they_do: They pass the app's own type definitions to the model as the output contract, then validate the response with the TypeScript compiler; on failure the compiler error is sent back to the model to retry.
takeaways.evidence_quote: that error message can be used to perform a repair when you are reaching out to a language model to say no no no no no that's not what I wanted try again

takeaways.technique: Schema engineering instead of prompt engineering
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than instructing the model with prose about formatting, they encode the desired shape in types and let the model fill it, including an explicit 'unknown text' field to capture input it could not map.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of doing this sort of prompt engineering you're doing schema engineering

takeaways.technique: Generated programs over a restricted typed API with refs
takeaways.what_they_do: For multi-step tasks they have the model emit a JSON 'fake language' of calls with refs to prior results, then build an in-memory typed program so only declared methods and type-matching arguments are permitted.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we generate a fake language uh we have the language models generate a fake language still based on the types

takeaways.what_they_do: They argue the type contract plus validation makes weaker or local models usable, since bad output is caught and repaired rather than trusted.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you use an a language model that is sufficiently trained on both human Pros natural language and code this actually Bridges the Two Worlds together

takeaways.what_they_do: They use the TypeScript compiler itself as the validator for model output, so correctness is checked by a real tool rather than by another LLM judgment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's actually using the types compiler under the hood
